intro: Ways to pay, seasonal sales, and everyday expressions about money.
p.estar sin blanca: to be broke; to have no money
p.estar sin blanca.nota: Colloquial. Blanca was also the name of a historical coin; the expression means having no money.
p.costar un ojo de la cara: to cost an arm and a leg
p.estar tirado.nota: Colloquial. Tirado agrees with the item: el precio está tirado, la chaqueta está tirada.
p.apretarse el cinturón: to tighten one's belt; to cut back
p.apretarse el cinturón.nota: The reflexive pronoun agrees with the subject: me aprieto el cinturón, nos apretamos el cinturón.
p.tirar la casa por la ventana: to spend lavishly; to spare no expense
p.ser un agarrado.nota: Informal and critical. Use agarrado for a man and agarrada for a woman.
p.mirar el dinero.nota: In no mirar el dinero, the negative phrase means not to worry about the cost.
p.la ganga: the bargain; a very good deal
p.al contado: in full; paid all at once
p.tacaño.nota: The adjective agrees with the person: tacaño, tacaña, tacaños, tacañas.
p.derrochador.nota: The adjective agrees with the person: derrochador, derrochadora, derrochadores, derrochadoras.
p.ahorrador.nota: The adjective agrees with the person: ahorrador, ahorradora, ahorradores, ahorradoras.
p.las tres bes: the three Bs: good, pretty and cheap
p.las tres bes.nota: A playful shopping slogan: bueno, bonito y barato.
b1.texto:
How you pay: **en efectivo**, **con tarjeta**, **a plazos**, or **al contado** (in full).

**Las rebajas** are seasonal sale periods; dates vary. You may see **un descuento del 30 %**, **una oferta** or **una ganga**. A good buy has **las tres bes**: **bueno, bonito y barato** (good, pretty and cheap).

Common informal expressions: **estar sin blanca** means to have no money; **costar un ojo de la cara** means to be very expensive; **estar tirado** means to be very cheap. **Apretarse el cinturón** means to cut back, while **tirar la casa por la ventana** means to spend lavishly. **Ser un agarrado/a** means to be stingy and can sound critical. **Mirar el dinero** means to watch one's spending; **no mirar el dinero** means not to worry about the cost.

Related descriptions: **tacaño/a** (stingy), **derrochador/a** (a big spender), **ahorrador/a** (thrifty; a saver).
b2.f0: I'm broke. This month I have to tighten my belt.
b2.f1: Well, look at these shoes. They're dirt cheap: twenty euros.
b2.f2: I like the other ones more, but they cost an arm and a leg.
b2.f3: You're so stingy! I spare no expense during the sales.
b2.f4: Of course, you pay by card and don't worry about the cost.
b2.f5: And you save so much that you never buy anything.
b4.o1.explicacion: Blanca was also the name of a historical coin; the expression means having no money.
b5.pregunta: Something is very expensive. Which idiom fits?
b5.o0.refuerzo: It costs an eye from your face.
b5.o1.refuerzo: That means it is very cheap.
b5.o2.refuerzo: That is about a person who spends a lot.
b6.pregunta: «Tirar la casa por la ventana» means…
b6.o0.refuerzo: To throw the house out of the window.
b7.o1.refuerzo: A card takes con: con tarjeta.
b8.pregunta: Complete: this month I have to tighten my belt.
b9.traduccion: These shoes cost an arm and a leg.
b10.texto:
**The app cannot check this part.** For the writing, please use pen and paper. For the speaking, say it out loud and, if you can, practise with a native speaker or a teacher who can correct you.

**Write (100–120 words).** Write about how you manage your money: what you spend most on and where you could save.

**Speak (about 2 minutes).** Explain to a friend aloud why you cannot lend them money, or agree with conditions.
b4.o0.explicacion: Estar sin blanca is slang for having no money at all.
